summary: An experimental document that defines metrics for measuring connectivity between a pair of Internet hosts, building on the IPPM framework in RFC 2330. It was replaced by RFC 2678.

plainLanguage.summary: This document describes ways to measure whether one computer can actually reach another across the internet, so people measuring it all count things the same way.

questions: how to test if hosts can reach each other
subtitle: Standard definitions for measuring whether packets can travel between two hosts

tldr.problem: Internet measurement researchers needed a common way to define and test whether data can travel between two hosts, without confusion from different definitions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2498 defines several connectivity metrics that build on each other: from simple one-way tests at a single moment, to two-way tests over time, to practical tests that measure whether a host can send and receive replies.
tldr.outcome: This experimental RFC was replaced by RFC 2678, but its framework for connectivity metrics remains important in network measurement.

today: RFC 2498 is Experimental and was replaced by RFC 2678. However, the framework defined here for connectivity metrics remains important in Internet measurement research and network monitoring practices.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Connectivity is the most basic capability of the Internet: two hosts must be able to reach each other to communicate. RFC 2498 defines metrics to measure it.

The RFC builds on the framework in RFC 2330, which covers general principles for measuring Internet performance. These metrics define connectivity in several layers of precision: first as an instantaneous test (can a packet get through right now?), then as measurement over time, and finally as the practical scenario most applications care about (can I send a message and get a reply back?).
sections.plainLanguage: The document is a rulebook for testing if computers can reach each other on the Internet. It starts simple (can a message go one way?) and gets more practical (can we have a conversation?).

sections.title: Instantaneous and Interval Connectivity
sections.content:
The simplest metric, Type-P-Instantaneous-Unidirectional-Connectivity, asks a single question: if we sent a packet from source address A to destination address B at time T, would it arrive? A yes or no answer is the metric.

Building on this, Type-P-Interval-Unidirectional-Connectivity extends the test over a time window. Instead of testing at one moment, it tests during a time interval [T, T+dT]. If a packet successfully traverses the path at any point within that interval, the answer is yes. The Internet Protocol Lifetime field (TTL) limits how long a packet can exist; the text notes this must be accounted for when measuring.
sections.plainLanguage: The first test is like asking: can a message get through right now? The second test is like asking: during the next 60 seconds, will at least one message get through? This matters because sometimes a router is briefly too busy.

sections.title: Two-way Connectivity and Practical Measurement
sections.content:
Bidirectional connectivity extends the unidirectional metrics: addresses A1 and A2 have two-way connectivity if A1 can reach A2 AND A2 can reach A1, both during the same time interval.

Most applications need more: they send a message and expect a reply. Type-P1-P2-Interval-Temporal-Connectivity captures this. A host at source address Src can send a P1 packet to destination address Dst, and later receive a P2 response packet back (the types can differ because replies might use a different protocol). The measurement must verify that a request packet was sent, a response was received, and the round-trip time fits within the measurement window.
sections.plainLanguage: Two-way connectivity means both directions work. Temporal connectivity is more practical: it means I can send a message and someone will send one back. This is what real applications need.

sections.title: Measurement Methodology and Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC sketches an algorithm to estimate temporal connectivity in practice. To test whether Src can reach Dst and get a reply, send N probe packets at random times across the measurement interval [T, T+dT]. Look for any reply packet arriving before time T+dT. If at least one reply arrives, connectivity is confirmed.

Recommended values are: measure over a 60-second interval (dT=60 seconds), wait up to 10 seconds for a reply (W=10 seconds), and send 20 probe packets (N=20). The RFC notes this is inexact—the algorithm cannot test every microsecond—but it provides practical guidance without burdening the network.
sections.plainLanguage: To test if you can reach a computer and get a reply, ping it 20 times over a minute. If you get any replies back, it works. Scientists can adjust this if they need more detail or less network traffic.

sections.title: Security and Practical Aspects
sections.content:
The document notes that active measurement (sending packets to test connectivity) can be abused for denial-of-service attacks if disguised as legitimate measurement. Additionally, testing for connectivity can reveal firewall policies and other security mechanisms to an attacker.

For TCP, the RFC details how to interpret responses: a SYN-ACK confirms connectivity and establishes a connection (which should be torn down cleanly), while RST or ICMP port-unreachable messages also confirm that the path works, even though no service is running on that port.
sections.plainLanguage: Pinging computers to test connectivity can be misused as an attack. Also, the RFC shows how to test using the same connection handshake TCP uses, so measurement tools can be practical instead of crude.
